title: UnitedHealth Stock Recovered Before Its Margins Did - Trefis
content:
UnitedHealth (UNH) stock has gained about 41% since early March, and at roughly $400 a share the market has already paid for a recovery. The easy reading is that the turnaround is finished. It is not. One half got better over those six months, the other got worse, and the price reflects the good half. Management planned 2026 around a Medicare medical cost trend of around 10% and now expects to land below it, though the trend is still running well above historical levels. The company names its own benefit design, care management models and network curation as the primary reason, with prior year development and a lighter respiratory season also helping. Medicare margins should finish 2026 above 3%, on a Medicare Advantage book set to shed roughly 1.1 million members. Optum Health did its work in care delivery rather than plan design. It runs primary and specialist care, ambulatory surgery and home health for 20 million people, and better support for patients moving between care settings has cut hospitalizations by about 10% in its Western and Southern regions since late last year. That is a cost the company took out itself. In the commercial business, medical cost trend is running modestly above the 11% management previously saw, and there is still no evidence of it moderating. Two of the drivers stand out. One is that providers are coding office visits and emergency department encounters more intensively. The other is the arbitration process created by the No Surprises Act: UnitedHealthcare noted that roughly 60% of all arbitration cases are brought by just five entities, with prevailing arbiter awards averaging 11 times what Medicare would pay. Management sizes that drag at about 50 basis points of incremental trend in 2026, and at least 100 basis points of total cost. Management now expects full margin recovery in the commercial book to take past 2027, against its own historic margin of 7% or greater for that group business. The half that has to close the gap now has longer to do it. UnitedHealth’s company-wide operating margin is 4.8%, against an average of 7.1% over the past three years. That gap is the investment case. In mid-July, adjusted 2026 earnings guidance moved to $19.50 to $20 a share, and the full-year operating-earnings outlook to at least $12 billion for UnitedHealthcare and at least $2.2 billion for Optum Health. Both operating-earnings figures are segment outlooks, not the whole company, and a market value near $360 billion is already paying for them. Elevance Health (ELV) returned 41.6% over the same six months, so UnitedHealth was not the only insurer repriced. But Cigna (CI) returned 4.7% over the same window, so the group did not move as one. The 2026 outlook has already been raised and the commercial cost trend has not turned. Whichever moves next decides the rest. You know why this one ran, and getting there meant taking the company apart segment by segment. Handing that work to a system is the alternative. title: Is UnitedHealth Finally Turning the Corner After a Tough 2025? - The Globe and Mail
content: UnitedHealth Group, Inc. UNH appears to be making meaningful progress toward recovering from the turbulence that weighed on its performance in 2025. After facing elevated medical costs, unfavorable utilization trends and pressure across government-sponsored businesses, the healthcare giant has entered 2026 with a stronger operating footing. In the first half of 2026, its total revenues rose 1.2% year over year along with 20.5% growth in adjusted earnings per share (EPS). A key catalyst has been better control over medical expenses. UNH’s medical care ratio declined to 86.7% in the second quarter from 89.4% a year earlier, aided by improved pricing, benefit-design changes, member mix, medical-cost management and favorable prior-period reserve development. The improvement helped UnitedHealthcare’s operating margin expand to 4.6% from 2.4% in the prior-year quarter. Meanwhile, membership declined, particularly in Medicare Advantage, as UNH is currently prioritizing profitable growth over enrollment expansion, a strategy that could support healthier margins over time. Optum is also contributing to the recovery. The segment benefited from improved operational execution, with operating income rising 29% year over year to $4 billion in the second quarter. Investments in technology, artificial intelligence and care-delivery capabilities are aimed at improving productivity and clinical efficiency, potentially creating additional opportunities for margin expansion. The stronger results encouraged UnitedHealth to raise its 2026 adjusted EPS outlook to $19.50-$20. Still, elevated medical-cost trends, pressure in Medicaid and commercial benefits and membership declines remain risks. Therefore, sustained medical-cost discipline and continued improvement at Optum will be crucial for making the recovery durable. Some of UNH’s major competitors in the medical space are Humana Inc.HUM and Elevance Health, Inc.ELV. Humana is focusing on pricing, network management and operating efficiencies to restore margins while navigating elevated medical costs and utilization across its Medicare Advantage business. In the first half of 2026, HUM’s adjusted revenues increased 24.9% year over year and adjusted EPS grew 0.3%. Elevance is prioritizing medical cost management, operating efficiency and Carelon’s expansion while dealing with elevated medical costs and membership declines in government businesses. In the first half of 2026, operating revenues increased 1.2% year over year, while adjusted EPS declined 3.7%. Shares of UNH have gained 28.7% in the past year compared with the industry’s growth of 24%. From a valuation standpoint, UnitedHealth trades at a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 18.46, above the industry average of 15.99. UNH carries a Value Score of B. title: Does the Gloom Finally End for New Hampshire? Season Preview - Sports Illustrated
content: It’s been a long time since UNH was one of the college hockey powers in Hocley East, and after the last few seasons it’s become a question of if, not when. Head coach Mike Souza is heading into his 9th season at the helm in Durham, and you’d have to imagine results must come fast for the Wakefield, Mass. native if he wants to hang on to his throne. The Wildcats haven’t made the NCAA Tournament since 2013 and have finished tenth in Hockey East in back-to-back seasons. Fortunately for the Wildcats, a roster that desperately needed revamping got some crucial additions during the offseason. UNH brought in seven transfers, including some firepower and goaltending help. With both Morgan Winters and Cy LeClerc graduating, the Wildcats went into the offseason without two of their top four scorers. They attempted to fill that hole with veterans Rasmus Svartström, Ryan Johnson and Nick VanTassell. Svartström is slightly the most impressive of the bunch. The Finland product tacked on 24 points for St. Lawrence last season in a surprisingly competitive ECAC, finishing second on the team in points. Meanwhile, Johnson helped lead the forward line for Alaska Anchorage, putting up 15 points, finishing second on the team in the category. VanTassell, though, offers a more complete package, coming over from UMass as one of the more physically active players on the ice. The Ottawa Senators prospect can play big, use his speed, add goals and has experience playing in the Hockey East. He started to put it together last year, but an injury held him back for a majority of the second half of the season. It’s a question mark whether he can get back to his late-2025 self, but if he does, UNH has a big-time addition. Souza and his staff put the biggest emphasis in the offseason on the goalie situation, where the Wildcats didn't return anyone. Kristian Coombs headed back to Canada, and both Kyle Chauvette and Jared Whale graduated. The coach replaced them with three players out the transfer portal. None of them raise eyebrows, but Teagan Kendrick is the one with the statistics and experience to start off the rip. He made 20 appearances for Sacred Heart last season and posted a 2.42 goals allowed average and a .920 save percentage. The Wildcats also brought in Michael Simpson from Providence and Stefan Carney from Division II to compete. Defensively, the Wildcats weren’t a bad unit in 2025-26. Despite finishing in the bottom half of the conference in goals allowed, they still had talent on the back end, and most of it is returning. Brendan Fitzgerald is undeniably the most notable player of the group. The senior finished third on the team in points, leading all Wildcat defenders in the category. He’s back as Souza’s No. 1 scoring defenseman. UNH also has Ryan Philbrick returning for his sophomore season after leading the team in blocks with 77. Along with Fitzgerald and Philbrick, Wildcat recruiting dipped into the OHL, the most prestigious level of the Canadian Hockey League, to grab two more on the blue line. Parker Von Richter is a Penguins prospect who scored 49 total points last season, and Wyatt Kennedy notched 26 points, including 23 assists, for the Windsor Spitfires. The recruiting didn’t conclude there as Souza and his staff added forwards from around North America. Mason Zebeski tallied 46 points in the OHL for multiple teams, Émile Guité, a Ducks prospect, added 65 points for the Chicoutimi Saguenéens of the QMJHL and Nicky Romeo put up 56 points for the Cedar Rapids RoughRiders in the USHL. After seasons of frustration and pain, it feels like UNH put together a formidable roster to compete with the rest of Hockey East, but a lot of things have to come together, and quickly. Will the goaltending be respectable? Will the freshmen hold their own? Can the transfers shake off their lack of experience in the conference? Often, when a team needs a lot of “ifs” to come true for success, things don’t go too well, and that could certainly be the case for the 2026-27 Wildcats. Expect them to be a tough team to beat, but one that finishes towards the bottom part of the conference once again. (UNH) jumped to 52-week highs on Thursday amid company-specific triggers, Wall Street optimism, and strong earnings results. AAPL stock closed up nearly 2% higher on Thursday as Apple Intelligence AI service registration in China, alongside Wall Street optimism over the company’s recent strength, bolstered prices. ATAI stock jumped more than 33% at close after Eli Lilly (LLY) confirmed that it is acquiring the clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company. Meanwhile, UNH stock gained more than 1% after its second-quarter (Q2) earnings blew past Wall Street estimates and it also raised its full-year profit outlook. Shares of the iPhone maker clocked an all-time high of $334.68 on Thursday amid a series of positive catalysts for the company. China's cyberspace regulator on Wednesday approved the registration of Apple Intelligence for use on iPhones in the country, clearing a key regulatory hurdle for the long-awaited launch of Apple's AI features in the country. Under Chinese rules, companies must obtain approval for large language models and generative AI services before releasing them to the public. Apple Intelligence is expected to leverage AI models from Baidu and Alibaba. Meanwhile, HSBC upgraded AAPL stock to ‘Buy’ from ‘Hold,’ with a price target of $366, implying an upside of 10% from the stock’s last close. Apple has drawn increased attention in recent weeks after it announced hikes in prices for several products, including MacBooks, iPads, HomePods and Apple TV devices, fueling speculation that iPhone price increases could follow. Investors are also focused on the company's upcoming leadership change, with John Ternus set to succeed Tim Cook as CEO on Sept. 1. AAPL stock has risen nearly 23% so far in 2026, while retail sentiment on Stocktwits was ‘bullish’ at the time of writing. Shares of the psychedelics company surged to a yearly high of $7.22 after pharma giant Eli Lilly (LLY) confirmed its acquisition of AtaiBeckley. Eli Lilly said that it will acquire all outstanding ATAI shares for $6.75 per share in cash, with shareholders eligible for an additional up to $2.50 per share if certain development and regulatory milestones are achieved, bringing the deal's total potential value to $9.25 per share. The cash offer represents a 25.9% premium to ATAI's Wednesday closing price, while the maximum consideration implies a 72.6% premium. The acquisition is expected to close in the third quarter (Q3) of this year. ATAI stock is up more than 84% this year. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment was in the ‘extremely bullish’ territory at the time of writing. UNH stock touched a 52-week high of $461.62 in Thursday’s trading session after its second-quarter (Q2) earnings results blew past Wall Street estimates. The company posted revenue of $112.03 billion, up about 0.37% from $111.62 billion in the prior-year quarter. However, it beat Wall Street expectations of $110.9 billion, as per Fiscal.ai estimates. Meanwhile, net income came in at $5.48 billion, or $6.04 per share, compared with $3.41 billion, or $3.74 per share, in the same period a year ago. The health insurer now expects 2026 adjusted earnings of $19.50 to $20 per share, up from its prior outlook of more than $18.25 per share, while maintaining its revenue guidance of more than $439 billion for the year. The company attributed the better-than-expected results and higher full-year profit outlook to improved management of elevated medical costs and greater use of AI to streamline operations. Shares of AST SpaceMobile (ASTS) suffered their worst one-day drop in more than two years on Thursday after a $1 billion convertible-note raise rattled investors, but options veteran Jon Najarian said that the deal still represents “a pretty strong bet to the upside.” ASTS stock plunged 17% on Thursday to close at $55.01, marking its lowest closing level of the year. Najarian and his brother Pete Najarian broke down the financing and ASTS’ selloff in a Market Rebellion video posted on X. The brothers co-founded Market Rebellion, an options-focused market analysis platform, in 2016. AST SpaceMobile priced $1 billion of 1.625% convertible senior notes due in 2034, with an initial conversion price of $79.57 per share, which was about 20% above Wednesday’s close. Jon Najarian said that the notes give buyers the right, but not the obligation, to convert into ASTS shares at that price. While the 1.625% coupon is relatively low, he said the real appeal lies in the potential equity upside. “If the stock’s 200 bucks, you’re still exercising it at $79.57,” he said, calling the structure “a pretty strong bet to the upside.” The $200 figure was a hypothetical example, not a formal price target. Pete Najarian said that investors were focused on the risk that the notes could eventually convert into shares and dilute existing holders. “They’re concerned about dilution and all the rest of it,” he said, adding that the stock’s negative reaction was “understandable.” Still, he agreed the financing could support a valuable long-term opportunity. “I think this could be something into the future that could be pretty special, quite frankly,” he said. The brothers also stressed that ASTS remains a highly volatile trade. Implied volatility in the options was around 100%, according to Pete Najarian. “The implied volatility of this thing is not a joke,” he said. “Hell yes, this thing is volatile.” AST SpaceMobile said proceeds remaining after capped-call transactions may be used to secure additional access to orbit through “partnerships and/or acquisitions.” The company said the move could further vertically integrate its business and reduce reliance on third-party launch providers, although it currently has no agreement for any transaction. Satellite communications analyst Tim Farrar said that the language pointed to a potential acquisition. Potential names raised included United Launch Alliance, Firefly Aerospace, Relativity Space and Stoke Space. Farrar also said that AST may be trying to copy Rocket Lab’s vertically integrated model across launch and satellite infrastructure. “ASTS were outbid for Iridium, so it looks like they are now trying to copy Rocket Lab’s vertical integration play,” he said. The Najarians also suggested acquisitions may be part of the plan. “They’ve got some ideas with partnerships, acquisitions, all that kind of thing that people are excited about,” Jon Najarian said. “They just needed the capital,” he added. The financing comes as AST SpaceMobile continues expanding its BlueBird satellite network. BlueBird 10 recently deployed its communications array in low Earth orbit, while BlueBirds 8 and 9 are next. BlueBird 11 has arrived at Cape Canaveral, and BlueBirds 12 and 13 are being transported from Texas to Florida. AST said that the newer satellites are expected to deliver nearly twice the peak speeds of its first-generation spacecraft. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for ASTS slipped to ‘neutral’ from ‘bullish’ levels a day ago amid ‘high’ message volume. The Syracuse Orange football team kicks off its season at home against New Hampshire Saturday, Sep. 3 at 12 p.m. ET. Orange fans looking to go to the season-opener are in luck, as tickets are available for as low as $4. Vivid Seats has plenty of tickets available for $4, all of which located in the 300-sections, or the highest section of the JMA Wireless Dome. While most are just selling two $4 tickets each, some sections are selling up to five or six tickets. Taking yourself and five family or friends to a Syracuse game could cost under $30 in section 311, which is directly behind the end zone. If you want a closer view of the game, it won’t require breaking the bank either. Tickets in the 100-sections — or the sections closest to the field — along the sideline are selling for under $30. Vivid Seats, SeatGeek and StubHub each have sub-$30 options along both sidelines in the 100-sections. For those willing to spend up in order to have the best game-viewing experience, there’s club seats in three different sections. In sections C101 and C130 (which are right next to each other) on the 50 yard line directly behind the Orange sideline. There’s also Club 44, located in section C108 right behind one of the end zones. The sideline club offers all-inclusive food and non-alcoholic beverages, along with four “alcoholic drink tabs”, cushioned seating access to the Kuhn Gameday Lounge and more. The 44 Club offers all-inclusive food and non-alcoholic beverages, two “alcoholic drink tabs”, cushioned seats and a direct view of Syracuse’s team tunnel. Section C130 in the sideline club has seats available for $307 on SeatGeek, which is the cheapest option you’ll find in either club seating section for Week 1. The Orange ended the 2025 season on a rough note, losing their final eight games after beginning the season 3-1, which included a win over Clemson. Syracuse finished the season 3-9, which was good for last in the ACC. The biggest reason for the drop off was starting quarterback Steve Angeli’s absence after he tore his Achilles in the 34-21 win over Clemson. In less than four games Angeli threw for 1,317 yards, 10 touchdowns and two interceptions. The Orange rotated through a few quarterbacks for the rest of the season, all of whom struggled. The non-Angeli quarterbacks combined for 1,290 yards, seven touchdowns and 13 interceptions.  carries into an announcement made in the second half of that widened access to child and family behavioral coaching across its commercial membership, reaching roughly thirteen million people. The move extends a service that had previously been available to a narrower group and places behavioral support alongside conventional medical benefits for a very large population. It arrives during a stretch in which the company has been reshaping how members and clinicians interact with its administrative machinery. A programme announced in the spring to remove prior authorization requirements from a substantial share of services continues toward completion by the end of this year, accompanied by a national gold card arrangement for clinician groups with consistent adherence to evidence-based guidelines. Taken together, these represent a deliberate repositioning of the administrative relationship between an insurer, its members and the clinicians who treat them. Behavioral coaching sits in the space between informal support and formal clinical treatment. It typically involves structured sessions with trained coaches who help families work through behavioural challenges, developmental concerns, school-related difficulties and the everyday stresses of parenting, without requiring a diagnosis or a referral into specialist mental health services. Extending that service to roughly thirteen million commercial members widens its reach substantially. The design point is early intervention: reaching families before difficulties escalate into situations requiring specialist psychiatric or psychological care, which are considerably scarcer and more expensive resources. The commercial book is where this kind of benefit design has the most immediate effect, because employer-sponsored plans compete partly on the breadth of services offered to employees and their dependants. Behavioral support for children and families has become one of the more requested additions in benefit consultations, reflecting how sharply demand in this area has risen. Access to behavioural and mental health care has become one of the most acute strains in the American health system. Waiting times for child and adolescent psychiatry can stretch across months in many regions. Clinician supply has not kept pace with demand, and geographic distribution is uneven, with rural and semi-rural areas particularly underserved. Demand meanwhile has risen sharply, especially among children and adolescents. Schools, paediatric practices and emergency departments have all absorbed cases that would ideally be handled in an outpatient behavioural setting. That mismatch produces poor outcomes and expensive downstream utilisation. Coaching services address part of the gap by handling needs that do not require a licensed clinician, freeing scarce specialist capacity for cases that do. They also scale differently from clinical services: coaches can be trained and deployed faster than psychiatrists, and delivery can be structured through virtual channels that overcome geographic constraints. The prior authorization programme announced in the spring commits to removing advance approval requirements from a substantial share of the services that previously carried them. The categories affected include selected outpatient surgical procedures, diagnostic tests such as echocardiograms, certain outpatient therapies and chiropractic care. The rollout is phased across the year, with a full list published for clinicians ahead of implementation. The company has framed the change around administrative burden. Prior authorization consumes clinician time, delays care and generates friction that members experience directly. Its stated position is that the mechanism should be reserved for situations where it genuinely protects patients rather than applied broadly. Company figures place prior authorization on a small minority of covered services, with the large majority of submitted requests approved within a day on average. Even so, the volume in absolute terms is enormous given the size of the membership, and the administrative load on clinical practices has become a prominent grievance across the profession. The gold card concept inverts the usual logic of utilisation management. Rather than applying the same approval requirements to every clinician, it identifies groups whose ordering patterns consistently align with evidence-based guidelines and exempts them from advance approval for the relevant services. The reasoning is that review effort should concentrate where variation from established practice is greatest, not spread evenly across clinicians whose behaviour is already well aligned. For qualifying practices, the effect is a meaningful reduction in administrative work and faster access for their patients. Implementation is not trivial. Determining which groups qualify requires reliable claims-based measurement, clear criteria and a mechanism for practices to understand and contest their status. Codes covered by the arrangement are periodically updated, and clinicians must track those updates to know where approval is still required. The enterprise operates through two broad arms. The insurance arm covers employer-sponsored plans, individual coverage, Medicare Advantage and managed Medicaid across a very large membership base. The health services arm spans pharmacy benefit management, care delivery through employed and affiliated clinicians, and data and technology services sold to external clients as well as used internally. That structure allows benefit design and care delivery to be coordinated in ways a standalone insurer cannot achieve. A behavioral coaching benefit, for instance, can be delivered through capabilities the group already owns rather than purchased from a third party. Pharmacy management can be integrated with medical benefit design. Care delivery assets can absorb volume that would otherwise flow to higher-cost settings. It also draws sustained scrutiny. Combining the payer and provider functions inside one enterprise raises questions about incentives that regulators, employers and clinicians examine closely, and the group operates under considerable public attention as a result. Pharmacy benefit management sits inside the health services arm and touches nearly every member the insurance arm covers. The function negotiates with manufacturers, builds formularies, operates mail and specialty pharmacy channels, and administers claims at the point of dispensing. At the scale involved, small changes in formulary placement or rebate arrangements translate into very large aggregate effects. The model has been under sustained examination. Critics argue that rebate-based arrangements create incentives favouring higher list prices, that the economics are opaque to employers and members, and that vertical ownership of pharmacies alongside benefit management raises conflicts. Defenders point to the negotiating leverage that scale provides and to the cost restraint it delivers relative to unmanaged drug spending. Whatever the merits, the practical position is that pharmacy arrangements have become a focus of legislative and regulatory attention, and several structural changes have been proposed across recent sessions. Companies operating in this space have begun adjusting their arrangements in anticipation, moving toward more transparent pricing models for some clients while retaining traditional structures for others. The health services arm employs and affiliates with a very large number of clinicians across primary care, urgent care, ambulatory surgery and home-based settings. That footprint makes the enterprise one of the largest employers of physicians in the country, entirely separate from its role as an insurer. The rationale is that value-based arrangements work better when the organisation bearing financial responsibility for outcomes also influences how care is delivered. Primary care capacity in particular determines whether chronic conditions are managed before they generate hospital admissions. Home-based assessment programmes identify unmet needs among members who rarely present to clinics. The structure also draws its sharpest criticism, since the same enterprise decides what is covered and provides the service being covered. Managing that tension transparently, and demonstrating that clinical decisions are made on clinical grounds, is a permanent governance requirement rather than a one-time exercise. Medicare Advantage has been the most turbulent part of the American health insurance market over the past several years. Medical cost trends ran ahead of the assumptions embedded in bids, utilisation among older members rose sharply after the pandemic-era trough, and reimbursement adjustments compressed margins across every major carrier. Carriers responded by withdrawing from unprofitable counties, trimming supplemental benefits and repricing plans. That repositioning has continued into the current planning cycle, with major carriers reporting that cost trends have become more manageable as pricing catches up with utilisation. The trade-off is membership: plans priced for margin recovery attract fewer enrollees, and county exits remove options for people who had chosen those plans. For an organisation with the largest Medicare Advantage membership in the country, that cycle matters enormously. It affects revenue, medical cost ratios and the composition of the membership that carries into subsequent years. The broader picture across healthcare stocks this year has been shaped by three forces. Utilisation trends in government-sponsored programmes have dominated the managed care segment. Obesity and metabolic therapies have transformed the pharmaceutical landscape and are beginning to reshape benefit design for payers who must decide how to cover them. And regulatory attention on pharmacy benefit arrangements, prior authorization practices and vertical integration has intensified across the industry. Managed care companies sit at the intersection of all three. They absorb the cost of new therapies, they administer the approval mechanisms under scrutiny, and they operate the integrated structures that regulators are examining. That makes them unusually sensitive to developments that originate elsewhere in the system. Meanwhile the underlying demographic force continues. The population eligible for Medicare grows every year, chronic disease prevalence rises, and the clinician workforce expands more slowly than demand. Those trends favour organisations with scale, data capability and care delivery assets, while intensifying the political attention such organisations attract. Alongside the prior authorization work, the company has run a pilot aimed at rural facilities across several states, with the stated aim of extending it nationally to reach a large number of rural hospitals. Rural providers face particular administrative strain because they operate with thin staffing and cannot dedicate personnel to approval processes the way large systems can. The group has also been extending community health hub arrangements through partnerships with academic health systems, placing services in communities where access has historically been limited. These initiatives serve a genuine access need and simultaneously address the reputational environment in which the company operates. The central operating variable for any managed care organisation is the relationship between premium revenue and medical costs. That relationship has been under pressure from several directions: higher utilisation of outpatient procedures, rising specialty pharmacy costs, behavioural health demand, and provider price increases negotiated into network contracts. Obesity and metabolic medicines deserve particular mention. Demand has been extraordinary, the medicines are expensive, and coverage decisions carry very large financial consequences at population scale. Payers have responded with varying combinations of eligibility criteria, formulary placement and cost sharing, and the arrangements remain in flux as oral formulations arrive and pricing shifts. Managing those pressures without degrading the member experience is the operating challenge. Removing administrative friction while controlling utilisation pulls in opposite directions, which is precisely why the gold card design, targeting review effort rather than applying it uniformly, has attracted attention. Underneath the insurance and services arms sits a data and technology function that processes claims, supports clinical decision tools, powers utilisation review and is sold to external health systems and payers as a standalone offering. At the volume involved, that data asset describes patterns across a substantial share of American medical encounters. Its practical uses are varied. Identifying members with unmanaged chronic conditions allows outreach before deterioration. Measuring clinician ordering patterns is what makes a gold card arrangement administrable at all. Detecting fraudulent or duplicative billing recovers meaningful sums. Supporting benefit design with actual utilisation evidence produces better-priced plans. The same capability attracts privacy scrutiny and questions about how algorithmic tools influence coverage decisions. Those questions have moved from academic discussion into active regulatory and legislative attention, and the standards applied to automated decision support in coverage determinations are still being formed. For those following the company's constituent position in the S&P 500, several observable items sit ahead. Completion of the prior authorization removal programme against its year-end schedule. Uptake of the expanded behavioral coaching benefit across the commercial book. Medicare Advantage plan positioning and county footprint for the coming enrolment cycle. Medical cost ratio movement in quarterly reporting. And the pace at which health services capabilities are deployed against benefit design. title: UNH deploys new underwater sensor system near Isles of Shoals - UnionLeader.com
content: A new tool to measure environmental conditions in the Gulf of Maine off New Hampshire’s shoreline is now up and running. Researchers at the University of New Hampshire and partners deployed acoustic and oceanographic sensors near the Isles of Shoals. The system is the first of its kind on the East Coast. Located 10 miles offshore and 3 miles east of Appledore Island, the system will transmit oceanographic and acoustic data in real time. “Measurements made with this valuable ocean asset will serve as a baseline for analyses of environmental conditions in this busy, productive area of the Gulf of Maine,” said Jennifer Miksis-Olds, director of UNH’s Center for Acoustics Research and Education and interim vice president for research and innovation. “This will expand our understanding of the ocean in real time.” The sensors will detect human and marine mammal activity, wind and precipitation, sea ice dynamics and oceanographic features, with implications for national security, energy development and commercial fisheries, officials said. The data is also expected to shed light on the connections between coastal measurements and the overall Gulf of Maine environment. Funded with a $6.2 million grant from the Office of Naval Research, the solar-powered system is composed of three elements: an underwater platform that hosts 10 sensors (hydrophones, 200 kHz echosounder, video, temperature, salinity, pH, dissolved oxygen, current, and chlorophyll sensors, and a fish tag receiver that will share detections with the Ocean Tracking Network), solar panel and data acquisition systems on Appledore Island, and a subsea cable that connects the two. Zachary Charewicz, director of facilities and sustainability at the Shoals Marine Laboratory, said panels and batteries on site help provide year-round power for the underwater listening array, which is tethered to the island via a subsea cable and powered by SML’s green grid. “They’re trying to get an idea of the undersea soundscape,” Charewicz said during a sustainability tour on Appledore Island in August. “There was some defense money involved in the funding — we are near a naval shipyard, you can kind of do the math on that one, why they might be interested. We’re taking not only sound readings but also water column readings.” The effort highlights partnerships between UNH and Newington-based SubCom, which donated and laid the cable; JASCO Applied Sciences, which designed the Underwater Listening System (ULS) platform and is a longstanding industrial partner of UNH’s Center for Acoustics Research and Education; and the Shoals Marine Laboratory. “The ULS has been an exceptional collaboration with Dr. Miksis-Olds and the teams at UNH, SubCom, and Ocean Specialists,” said Bruce Martin, director of applied sciences at JASCO. “By delivering a continuous stream of acoustic, biological, and oceanographic data, the system will give students, researchers, and the public a powerful new window into how this corner of the Gulf of Maine changes across seasons and years.” “You’re sending light pulses down the cable, those light pulses are bouncing back from the other end, or in the case of distributed acoustic sensing, as a sound wave moves through the water and interacts with the cable, it causes a minute deflection of that cable,” Charewicz said. “That light that’s traveling down will bounce off that deflection and go back to a receiver. Basically, what that allows you to do is determine where on the cable that sound was received, and the amplitude and general shape of the sound.” The system will extend the listening power of the Acoustic and Environmental Observation Network in the NW Atlantic (AEON), also led by Miksis-Olds. AEON acoustically covers the offshore waters of the Gulf of Maine from Cape Cod to the Bay of Fundy and east into Georges Bank, approximately 62 miles offshore; this new system will fill the coastal gap, providing full regional coverage and connectivity of the two systems. Data generated by the coastal ocean observing system will be accessible and open to all via a dedicated website. The federal program is currently channeling an estimated $3.6 billion to insurers this year to keep Part D premiums in check. Officials told The Wall Street Journal that the support will expire after 2026 and will not be extended into 2027. The Journal states that about 25 million Americans are enrolled in Part D plans, with the average monthly premium this year running near $36. The Wall Street Journal reports the decision could leave many seniors confronting higher premiums for their stand-alone prescription coverage beginning in 2027. Without the federal support, plan sponsors may pass increased costs to enrollees, potentially accelerating shifts toward Medicare Advantage plans that bundle drug benefits. An administration official quoted by the Journal projected that roughly one-quarter of Part D enrollees will see their premiums hold steady or decline in 2027, about 30% will face hikes under $10 a month, and the remaining 45% will largely see increases in the $11–$20 range. The subsidy primarily benefits insurers offering stand-alone Part D plans (PDPs). Companies with substantial PDP enrollment—UnitedHealth Group (UNH), CVS Health (CVS, via Aetna), Humana (HUM), Centene (CNC, via WellCare), and Molina Healthcare (MOH)—stand to lose this revenue stream. Loss of the $3.6-billion in support could pressure margins if insurers absorb costs or reduce competitiveness through higher premiums, risking enrollment declines. However, beneficiaries might also migrate to Medicare Advantage plans and help offset losses. Centene holds the largest share of stand-alone Medicare Part D (PDP) enrollment via Wellcare — more than eight million members as of early 2026, or about one-third of the entire PDP market, exceeding the exposure of its rivals. In a major bid to accelerate American dominance in the commercial space sector, the Trump administration announced a proposal allowing the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to bypass lengthy environmental reviews for rocket launches, spacecraft reentries, and commercial launch site approvals. The initiative, announced on Tuesday by Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy, aims to eliminate red tape for commercial operators as the U.S. prepares for an unprecedented surge in orbital launches and space infrastructure development. Commercial space stocks, including Rocket Lab (RKLB), AST SpaceMobile (ASTS), Intuitive Machines (LUNR), and Planet Labs (PL) dropped between 3% and 7% on Tuesday, while SpaceX (SPCX) added 3%. Under the proposed framework, the FAA would gain the authority to waive requirements established across 13 major federal environmental statutes. These include the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), the Endangered Species Act, the Clean Water Act, and the Clean Air Act. Federal officials emphasized that exemptions would only apply where environmental rules delay innovation, maintaining that core public health, national security, and safety safeguards will remain intact. "America won the first Space Race, and we can do it again -- but only if we get government red tape out of the way," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy stated, noting that the goal is to lower costs and strengthen U.S. competitiveness. Environmental assessments—which currently can take over a year to complete—have long been a target of frustration for commercial launch providers. While conservation groups view these evaluations as crucial for protecting coastal wildlife habitats, launch companies have repeatedly slammed the reviews as duplicative administrative bottlenecks. The FAA's proposal opens a 30-day public comment window before final rules are enacted. The drive to deregulate comes as the commercial space industry experiences exponential growth. The FAA reported authorizing a record 204 commercial space operations in FY2025. Over the next decade, federal forecasts project total operations could reach over 4,200, climbing from 214 this year to more than 500 annual operations by 2036. Much of this growth is being driven by heavyweights like Elon Musk’s SpaceX, Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin, Rocket Lab, and rising startups like Stoke Space. These firms are aggressively deploying satellite constellations for broadband connectivity, defense applications, and orbital data centers. title: New UNH road construction training program aims to address workforce shortage - nhpr.org
content: The Federal Highway Administration has awarded a $250,000 grant to the University of New Hampshire to improve the state’s highway construction workforce training. The new training program is designed to create a pipeline for private employers and municipalities who desperately need more workers to help build highways, bridges and other infrastructure. The workforce shortage isn’t specific to New Hampshire. Nationally, 89% of construction firms said they struggled to find qualified workers despite a constant demand for road construction projects, according to UNH’s Technology Transfer Center. “Our biggest client is the [NH Department of Transportation],” Cody McGraw, a construction superintendent with the Plymouth-based company RM Piper, said. At times the company has struggled to maintain enough workers to complete state transportation projects while staying on budget and meeting the deadline. “There's a ceiling in which you can't accomplish jobs without more people than what you have,” McGraw said. A shortage of workers can lead to bridge or road construction projects going over budget and dragging on far longer than planned. McGraw also said the workforce as a whole is aging, and existing workers are at risk of burnout. The new UNH training program will have two tracks to grow the workforce: one focused on teaching adults seeking a career change, and the other for high school students to learn about the potential careers in the transportation construction industries. Marilee Enus, the director of UNH’s Technology Transfer Center that will run the program, said many high schoolers, even those enrolled in trade programs, don’t know that highway construction is a career path. “Everybody kind of grows up knowing what a doctor does,” Enus said. “Many young people never meet the people who design or build or maintain the transportation system.” The high school track will have about 15 people in a cohort starting this October and going through next year, where they’ll have monthly training sessions and a week of field work on construction sites. The adult track is tentatively scheduled to begin in December and will be an entry-level course in skills highway construction employers are looking for: heavy equipment awareness, work zone safety, knowledge of roadway materials and environmental considerations on site. Brooke Hayward is a construction superintendent with Pike Industries in Belmont; she started as a traffic coordinator after spending years as a paraeducator in elementary schools. She said that the UNH training can set someone up for success, but most employers will teach you on the job. “There's so many [positions] you can try,” Hayward-Miller said. “And with the shortage of help, there's a lot of opportunity in the construction field. Not everyone has to be a laborer.” NHPR is nonprofit and independent. We rely on readers like you to support the local, national, and international coverage on this website. Shares of Rivian Automotive (RIVN) fell 1% on Thursday after closing higher for ten consecutive sessions, as the company gears up for customer deliveries of its R2 mid-size SUV. Despite the slump on Thursday, the stock is on track to close its third consecutive week in the green, if gains hold. External customer deliveries and test drives of the more affordable midsize R2 SUV are slated to begin June 9 at Rivian showrooms and service centers across the U.S. The R2, priced from approximately $45,000 for the cheapest variant, is Rivian’s first mass-market model and is designed to compete directly with vehicles like Tesla’s best-selling Model Y. Rivian’s other offerings, including the R1T electric truck and the R1S electric SUV, are priced above $70,000 and cater to a more premium customer base. R2’s online configurator now shows three variants, namely standard, premium, and performance, priced between $48,490 and $57,990. Deliveries will commence with the Performance variant, followed by the Premium variant slated for later this year, and the Standard variant, which is slated to be launched next year. Talking about the company's launch plan, Rivian CFO Claire McDonough said at the UBS Auto and Auto Tech Conference on Wednesday that a select group of existing reservation holders will receive the option to configure their launch edition vehicles on June 9. McDonough said the streamlined launch is designed to shrink the time between order and delivery while managing customer expectations. “We’re just inviting customers that are interested in configuring their Launch Edition version of the vehicle to configure that, order that, so we can also shrink down the timeline between order and delivery and better manage expectations within the order bank of customers as well.” The company is intentionally limiting the initial offering to simplify execution. “It’s part of an overall strategy of how do you go slow to go fast,” McDonough explained. “In doing so, we’ve cultivated a smaller assortment of our launch variant product, which is our performance variant, which has a number of additional bundled features included as part of it that we’ll launch with.” That Launch Edition bundles lifetime autonomy, a tow package, and other features that will later become optional add-ons. For the whole of 2026, Rivian now expects to deliver 62,000-67,000 vehicles, up from the 42,247 vehicles delivered in 2025. However, the bulk of this guidance will be weighted towards the fourth quarter, McDonough clarified at the conference. “As we think about the overall execution of the ramp, it’s heavily going to be supply chain driven,” McDonough said. “Our teams have spent a lot of time with each and every one of our suppliers… you can only ramp as quickly as your weakest supplier.” Despite the measured rollout, McDonough expressed strong confidence in the underlying demand for the R2, noting earlier this week that the R2 targets the largest and fastest-growing segment in the industry—the five-passenger SUV and crossover space—and is positioned to attract both loyal Rivian customers and first-time EV buyers. Shares of General Motors (GM) jumped 2% on Thursday following reports that it has rehired more than 100 former employees from its now-defunct Cruise autonomous-vehicle subsidiary as it advances the development of “eyes-off” self-driving technology aimed at personally owned vehicles rather than robotaxis. The rehiring comes roughly eighteen months after GM effectively shut down Cruise in December 2024, when the company stopped funding the unit’s robotaxi ambitions, folded its technology and some of its staff into GM’s broader technical teams, and pivoted resources toward enhancing its existing Super Cruise advanced driver-assistance system. GM has rehired its former employees from firms including Nvidia, Uber, and Zoox, The Information reported. It reflects GM’s decision to develop fully autonomous vehicles for consumers’ personal use, GM’s vice president of autonomous vehicles, Rashed Haq, told The Information, adding that the company is not resuming its driverless ride-hailing business under Cruise. In August, Bloomberg had reported on GM’s efforts to bring back former Cruise employees. Cruise was a major robotaxi player in Waymo's leagues until October 2023, when a Cruise robotaxi got involved in an accident in San Francisco, giving rise to heightened regulatory scrutiny, the exit of high-profile executives, including co-founder Kyle Vogt, and the suspension of robotaxi services. A few months later, GM said it was abandoning its plans to build the pedal-less Origin autonomous vehicle and said it would instead use its next-generation Chevrolet Bolt for autonomous driving purposes. Still, by December 2024, the company announced Cruise’s closure. The robotaxi development work needs considerable time and resources to scale, GM reasoned, while adding that the market is getting increasingly competitive. The company had said it would instead work on the progress of Super Cruise, its hands-off, eyes-on driving feature, deployed in passenger vehicles, and let go of about 1000 employees. GM’s reconstituted group will debut an electric Cadillac in 2028 that lets drivers go eyes-off and hands-free on highways, with more models to follow, The Information said. Later versions will add eyes-off autonomy in cities, eventually eliminating the need for anyone to sit in the driver’s seat. “Everybody in the car will be a passenger,” Haq reportedly said. “Nobody will need to be in charge of any of the driving tasks—you’ll even be able to send it on mobility errands.” The plan is similar to Ford’s BlueCruise, a system that allows for hands-free driving on certain highways in select Ford and Lincoln vehicles. title: OSI Completes Subsea Cable Work For UNH Appledore Acoustic Array In Gulf Of Maine - Ocean News & Technology
content: Ocean Specialists, Inc. (OSI), an Advanced Ocean Systems company, has successfully completed its technical and operational support role in the deployment of the University of New Hampshire's (UNH) Appledore Acoustic Array, an advanced coastal monitoring system installed off the coast of Appledore Island in the Gulf of Maine. The Ocean and Acoustic Observation System enhances regional ocean research capabilities by enabling high-resolution acoustic monitoring for environmental studies, fisheries science, national security, and long-term ecosystem assessment. OSI’s scope encompassed pre-deployment engineering review, cable route assessment and survey, installation planning, and the design, procurement, installation, and commissioning of the terrestrial and subsea cable/fiber terminations. The team also conducted detailed reviews of vessel and deck operations and supported final system integration to verify full continuity and operational readiness of the array. “Supporting UNH on the Ocean and Acoustic Observation System project reflects OSI’s commitment to advancing ocean science through reliable subsea systems engineering,” said Perry Wright, President of OSI. “Our team brought decades of experience in subsea cable systems, marine operations, and coastal infrastructure to ensure a safe, efficient, and technically robust installation.” The successful deployment marks a significant milestone for UNH’s coastal research initiatives, expanding the university’s ability to collect continuous ocean and acoustic data critical to understanding changing ocean conditions in the Gulf of Maine. “We value the collaboration with Ocean Specialists Inc.,” said Jennifer Mikis-Olds, Interim Vice President for Research and Innovation and Research Professor in the UNH Center for Acoustics Research & Education. “Their subsea expertise and operational leadership were essential to delivering this system safely and effectively.” With the Ocean and Acoustic Observation System operational, UNH and regional partners will initiate systematic data acquisition to underpin marine research initiatives, guide fisheries decision-making, support security-focused studies, and maintain continuous environmental surveillance.
